opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core insight was that code is really the natural action space for a large language model like GPT-4. These models have read enormous amounts of code on the internet, and they're remarkably good at writing it. So instead of asking the model to output low-level motor commands, like press this key or move the mouse by so many pixels, which is something it's never really seen in its training data, we let it write programs that call into a high-level Minecraft API.

Code also has some really nice properties for an agent that's meant to keep learning. First, it's compositional. Once Voyager writes a function to, say, craft a wooden pickaxe, it can call that function later inside a more complex program, like mining iron and smelting it. So skills build on top of skills, and you get this growing hierarchy of capabilities.

Second, code is interpretable and reusable. We store every working program in what we call a skill library, indexed by an embedding of its description. When Voyager runs into a new situation, it retrieves the relevant skills and reuses them, rather than relearning from scratch. That's a big part of why it doesn't suffer from catastrophic forgetting the way a neural network trained with gradient descent would.

And third, code gives you a clean feedback loop. When a program fails, you get an error message or feedback from the environment, like "you don't have enough wood," and the model can read that, reason about what went wrong, and rewrite the code. We called it iterative prompting. It's a form of self-improvement that happens entirely in context, no weight updates at all.

So the way I think about it, Voyager is doing lifelong learning, but the "parameters" being learned are a library of code rather than neural network weights. That was a fun reframing, and it turned out to work surprisingly well. Voyager explored much farther and unlocked the tech tree, up to diamond tools, much faster than prior methods.

The limitation, of course, is that it relies on a high-level API. It works for Minecraft because we can abstract away the low-level control. For robotics in the physical world, you can't just write "pick up the cup" and have it happen, so you still need models that handle the fine-grained motor control underneath. But as a way to get reasoning and long-horizon planning into an agent, code turned out to be a really powerful abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thinking really came from a simple question: what is the most expressive action space we can give a language model? If you look at the typical way people build agents in Minecraft, you have low-level controls, like move forward, turn left, attack. That's a very impoverished interface for an LLM. The model has to reason over thousands of tiny steps just to do something like chop a tree, and language models are honestly pretty bad at that kind of fine-grained motor control.

Code, on the other hand, is compositional. It has loops, conditionals, functions, abstractions. When GPT-4 writes a JavaScript function that says "find the nearest oak log, walk to it, mine it, repeat until you have ten," that one function encapsulates what would otherwise be hundreds of primitive actions. And more importantly, the model is already extremely good at writing code, because it's seen a huge amount of it during pretraining. So we're playing to its strengths rather than its weaknesses.

The second piece, which I think is actually the more interesting part, is that code is a natural format for a skill library. Once Voyager writes a function that works, say, "craft a stone pickaxe," we store it, and the next time the agent needs it, it can just call that function instead of rediscovering it from scratch. Skills build on skills. The pickaxe function calls the mining function, which calls the navigation function. So you get this ever-growing library of executable knowledge, and that's really what enables the lifelong learning aspect. The agent gets more capable over time, not because we're updating weights, but because the library of programs keeps expanding.

And the last thing is that code gives you a very clean feedback loop. If the program fails, you get a stack trace, you get an error message, and the model can read that and self-correct. That's much harder to do when your actions are just raw keypresses. So code ended up being the right abstraction on basically every axis: expressiveness, reusability, and debuggability.

The thinking was that code gives the agent a way to express actions at a much higher level. In Minecraft, something like crafting a tool can involve a long sequence of movements and interactions. Instead of having the language model decide every button press, we can have it write a program that carries out that sequence, with loops, conditionals, and feedback from the environment.

And code is compositional. Once the agent has a working program for a useful skill, it can save that skill and call it later as part of something more complex. It doesn’t have to figure everything out from scratch each time. That gives us a way to build up a growing library of capabilities.

It also creates a natural feedback loop: generate code, run it, see what failed, and revise it. So code is both the interface for acting in the world and a way to represent skills that the agent can improve and reuse.

You want it to write a program that carries out that behavior, using feedback from the environment to debug and improve it.

And the really useful part is that code is reusable. Once Voyager figures out how to do something, it can save that program in a skill library. Later, it can retrieve that skill and compose it with other skills to solve a more complicated task. So it doesn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch. Code becomes a way to turn experience into capabilities that accumulate over time.
